title: B-tree (balanced search tree)
summary: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree data structure that maintains sorted data and allows O(log n) search, insert, and delete. Each node has between t-1 and 2t-1 keys (t = minimum degree). All leaves are at the same level. Used in databases (indexes), filesystems (ext4, XFS, Btrfs), and key-value stores.

structure.meaning: Each node: n keys + n+1 child pointers (for internal nodes) or n keys + n+1 record pointers (for leaf nodes). Keys are sorted.
Each node has at least t-1 keys (except root: at least 1) and at most 2t-1 keys. Each internal node has at least t children and at most 2t children.
Binary search within node, then recurse to child. O(log_t n) node accesses.
Find leaf, insert key. If node is full (2t-1 keys), split it (median key moves up to parent). May cascade to root.
Find key, remove. If node underflows (< t-1 keys), borrow from sibling or merge with sibling. May cascade to root.
All data in leaves; internal nodes only store keys for routing. Leaves linked in a doubly-linked list for range scans. Used by most databases.
Nodes are 2/3 full before splitting (vs 1/2 for B-tree). Reduces splits.

notes: B-trees are the foundation of database indexes and filesystem metadata.
B+ trees store all data in leaves (linked list) for efficient range scans.
B-tree node size matches disk block size (4KB) for optimal I/O.
B-trees are used by PostgreSQL, MySQL (InnoDB), SQLite, ext4, XFS, Btrfs, and many others.
LSM trees (Log-Structured Merge) are an alternative for write-heavy workloads.
